World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Three dead in boating accident off NSW coast
World.content:
Three people have died after a boating accident at Ballina off the northern NSW coast, with a search continuing for survivors.

Emergency services were contacted about 6:15pm on Monday, after a report a yacht appeared to be having difficulties off the South Ballina break wall.

Marine Rescue NSW responded, but their vessel rolled while crossing the Ballina Bar in heavy conditions.

In a statement, NSW Police said three people had died, while four made it to shore.

It is unknown how many people were on the yacht, which police now believe has sunk.

Tweed Heads Water Police and general duties officers from Richmond Police District are on scene.

Marine Area Command is conducting a search-and-rescue effort from their Balmain headquarters, which will resume this morning.

The four people injured are being checked by NSW Ambulance paramedics, but none are believed to have life-threatening injuries.

Additional assistance will be provided by the AMSA Challenger jet and Westpac Rescue Helicopter from Lismore.

World.title: Three main issues set to sway voters in Qld by-election
World.content:
Battle lines for a state by-election in Brisbane's north have been drawn on fuel, health, and the cost of living.

Early voting opens today for the more than 41,000 voters in the Stafford electorate, ahead of polling day on May 16.

The contest was sparked by the death of independent MP Jimmy Sullivan, whose body was found at his home in non-suspicious circumstances last month.

The 44-year-old had sat on the crossbench after he was ousted from the Labor caucus last year, following scrutiny over his personal life.

Stafford, encompassing suburbs including Kedron, Chermside, and Stafford Heights, is Labor heartland.

Residents are largely young families, renters, and tertiary educated.

Issues front of mind for voters' echo those felt across Queensland.

Voters (L-R) Kyle Daniel, Anthony Williamson and Sharon Wootton say they're worried about rising living costs. (ABC NEWS: Mark Leonardi)

"Fuel costs, housing costs, and food costs, all going up at the moment," local Anthony Williamson told the ABC.

"Fuel prices, they keep going up, rates as well," Sharon Wootton said.

"Cost of living, definitely, public transport is unreliable as well," Kyle Daniel said.

'Cutting to the bone'

Sullivan won Stafford in the 2024 state election with a margin of more than 5 per cent, and Labor has held it for nine of the last 10 polls.

Luke Richmond, the party's recent Queensland assistant state secretary, is hoping to continue that dominance.

Labor candidate for Stafford Luke Richmond wants to extend the party's dominance in the seat. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

The lawyer wants to make the contest a referendum on health.

"The LNP are a government that said they weren't going to make cuts to health, but the reality is that they are cutting to the bone," he said.

"People are really frustrated with a government that they see as being all talk and no action, all photo op, no follow-up."

Kos Samaras, pollster and director of the RedBridge Group, said Labor should "hold the seat comfortably".

"It's a very progressive part of Brisbane and increasingly becoming so. The left side of politics in this seat is quite significant."

Fuel focus for LNP

LNP candidate Fiona Hammond and the government was squarely focused on the fuel crisis.

Premier David Crisafulli announced the date of the by-election from a service station and for several weeks spruiked his team's efforts on fuel security.

Ms Hammond, a former Brisbane City councillor, contested the last state election, recording a more than 6 per cent swing to the LNP.

LNP candidate for Stafford Fiona Hammond says Queenslanders want fuel security. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

She said there were three main things on Stafford locals' minds.

"They're talking about fuel security. They're talking about the cost of living, and they're also talking about crime.

"We want us to have our own fuel reserves right here in Queensland, so we're not reliant on overseas fuel."

Mr Samaras said any further significant swing to the LNP in the by-election would be "quite seismic".

"That will indicate that they are starting to make inroads into Brisbane," he said.

"The LNP is doing really well outside of Brisbane, but in places like this, in seats like this, the Labor Party is still holding up its primary vote."

The LNP has historically faced an uphill battle to take the Stafford seat. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

No preference deal for the Greens

Also throwing her hat in the ring for another tilt is Jess Lane of the Greens.

The teacher won a healthy 18 per cent primary vote at the last state election and said there was one main thing residents were concerned about.

Jess Lane, from the Greens, wants to impose rent caps to help with the cost of living. (Supplied)

"Cost of living hands down, particularly around housing and rents," she said.

"We're going to be fighting to cap rents and improve the cost of living for families who are really doing it tough in the community."

The Greens will not be directing voters on how to preference their votes.

One Nation steers clear

A notable absence in a crowded field of nine candidates is One Nation.

Leader Pauline Hanson said the party's focus was on the next state election in 2028.

Mr Samaras described Stafford, and seats like it, as having a "demographic barrier" for the surging minor party.

"Anything that is in an urban area with high numbers of young professionals, a very large number of people who are renting, is obviously very difficult political terrain for them," he said.

World.title: What to know as another round of train disruption begins in Queensland
World.content:
Queensland commuters could face ongoing delays as hundreds of train services are paused from today "until further notice".

It comes amid ongoing industrial action, with negotiations over a new enterprise agreement at a standstill.

Here's what you need to know.

Which services are affected?

From Tuesday May 5, trains will run on a reduced timetable, with weekday services to run at a schedule similar to a Saturday.

It amounts to a 20 per cent cut in services, with 273 fewer trains operating on weekdays.

During peak hours, trains will run every 15 minutes on the Caboolture, Cleveland, Ferny Grove, Gold Coast, Ipswich, Redcliffe Peninsula and Springfield lines.

That's a reduction from the normal timetable, which has services operating every 6-10 minutes.

Commuters have been warned to expect busier trains with lines set to run at a weekend-style service for at least the rest of the week. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Services will run every 30 minutes on the Beenleigh and Shorncliffe lines, and on the Doomben line between Doomben and Eagle Junction.

Services will also run every 30 minutes between Rosewood and Ipswich and on the Sunshine Coast between Nambour and Caboolture.

Queensland Rail said most trains will operate roughly every 30 minutes outside of peak hours.

Airtrain services are not affected by the changes.

Queensland Rail has urged commuters to check TransLink journey planner before travelling.

Regional services will also be affected.

Spirit of Queensland will continue to run between Brisbane and Townsville, but a coach service will operate between Townsville and Cairns.

The Westlander remains cancelled, replaced by Greyhound services.

Spirit of the Outback eastbound services will continue from Longreach to Mount Larcom, skipping Rockhampton. Rockhampton passengers will be transferred from Mount Larcom.

Transport minister Brent Mickelberg says the changes will have a "considerable impact" on Queenslanders. (ABC News)

Why is this happening?

Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg and Queensland Rail have laid the blame on the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU), the Australian Manufacturing Workers Union (AMWU) and the Electrical Trades Union.

The RTBU announced it would take industrial action from today over stalled negotiations on a new enterprise agreement.

A Queensland Rail offer of an 8 per cent pay rise over three years was knocked back by the union last week.

Branch secretary of the Queensland RTBU, Peter Allen, said the union had announced partial work bans which they had given "quite a lot of notice for".

"It appears that Queensland Rail want to head down the track that they went just before Easter where they seem to want to lock our people out again," he said.

How long will this go for?

On Friday, Mr Mickelberg said the reduced services would be "temporary changes", but no end date had been set yet.

Negotiations are expected to continue this week.

Queensland Rail CEO Kat Stapleton has called on unions to stop their action.

"Queensland Rail wants to run a full timetable, but we can't do that during this continued union protected industrial action," she said.

Kat Stapleton has urged the union to call off its industrial action. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

"A reduced timetable is the best way to ensure as many services as possible can operate with the limited number of trains that we have available."

Queensland Rail and the unions will meet with the Fair Work Commission on Thursday in an attempt to address the breakdown in negotiations.

The Electrical Trades Union's Darren Wood said union frustration had been heightened in recent days after members taking part in limited strike action, such as partial work stoppages or bans, were told they would not be paid at all by Queensland Rail.

He said Queensland Rail's fleet of available trains had been severely limited as a result, and their position was unsustainable.

" They're going to have to either have our workers back and cut a deal, or the network's not going to run. "

A spokesperson for Queensland Rail said it would give customers "as much notice as possible" if any further changes are made to the network.

However, they said union action would not shut down the network entirely.

World.title: Luai's shock NRL move means Australian and NZ rugby must be 'on their toes'
World.content:
In the wake of Jarome Luai's announcement he will join the PNG Chiefs, Wests Tigers coach Benji Marshall revealed what he and the rest of the NRL were thinking.

"Every club needs to be on their toes," Marshall told reporters.

The Chiefs are making no apologies for their ambitious recruitment drive ahead of their inaugural NRL season in 2028, as they dangle lucrative tax-free salaries in front of players from the existing 17 clubs.

On ABC radio last Sunday, Chiefs general manager Michael Chammas declared Luai's signing would trigger a "snowball effect", with more players expected to follow suit.

Luai's shock move illustrates how aggressive player recruitment is becoming as the NRL expands to 19 teams (Perth Bears join the league next year).

The race for talent has intensified, which also has ramifications for rugby in Australia and New Zealand.

They must also be "on their toes" in the same way Marshall warned NRL clubs to be vigilant.

The best players emerging from rugby's junior ranks have been in the NRL's crosshairs for some time, and will continue to be, as 19 clubs look to fill roster spots and pathway squads.

Australia's junior rugby talent has been a target for NRL clubs. (Getty Images/Rugby Australia)

Adding to the challenge is the fact rugby and league co-exist in the "dual athlete" era at the underage level, meaning a considerable number of players are involved in both sports.

The term "code-agnostic" has been used in New Zealand to describe this situation.

Across the Tasman, there is increasing concern about rugby's ability to hold onto its juniors and attract the best talent to the game amid the opposition it faces from the rival code.

The Warriors' popularity is surging, and the NRL is strongly considering a second New Zealand-based franchise as part of its future expansion plans.

If dyed-in-the-wool Australian rugby fans scoff at the threat the NRL poses when it comes to player recruitment, they only needed to watch Manly's clash with Penrith on Sunday night.

Rising Manly star Joey Walsh represented Australia in rugby at the under-18 level. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Helping to pilot the Sea Eagles' attack in the halves was Joey Walsh, who played fly half for the Australian Schools and U18s rugby team in 2023.

The 19-year-old gave a glimpse of his ball-playing ability, producing a brilliant offload in the lead-up to the Sea Eagles' second try in their 18-16 loss to the Panthers.

Walsh is just one of many NRL players who grew up playing the two codes.

Rugby Australia (RA) is in its best position in decades to bankroll player retention strategies and invest in junior pathways after announcing a $70.6 million surplus and cash reserves of $31.4 million for the 2025 financial year.

It can also look forward to the windfall that will come with hosting the respective men's and women's Rugby World Cups in 2027 and 2029.

RA has wisely outlined there will be no reckless spending, suggesting it has learned from past mistakes.

But when RA does loosen the purse strings, funding ways to keep its best juniors in rugby must be a priority.

Ex-NRL stars face off

As NRL expansion bubbles away, two of its former stars were used as poster boys during Super Rugby Pacific's round 12 last week.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Zac Lomax were front and centre in the promotion of the NSW Waratahs' clash with the Western Force in Sydney on Friday night.

It was a smart move to drum up interest outside of rusted-on rugby followers.

But if any diehard NRL fans watched on TV or were among the 10,096 spectators who attended the match, they witnessed a lacklustre contest that went the way of the Force, 20-17.

Even Force coach Simon Cron admitted it was a "tough watch", while also describing his side's win as "ugly".

Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii played his first match for the Waratahs since early March. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Neither Suaalii nor Lomax had an impact, although there were limited opportunities for the ex-NSW State of Origin teammates as the match was a slog.

Importantly, however, Suaalii got through 59 minutes unscathed in his first appearance since injuring his hamstring before the Waratahs' round-four match against the Hurricanes in early March.

He needs match fitness under his belt ahead of a heavy Test season with the Wallabies, and will benefit from the run against the Force.

Time on the field is also vital for Lomax, as he navigates the early stages of his rugby journey.

He made mistakes against the Waratahs, such as a no-look pass that went into touch, but will learn from the experience.

When positioned on the blindside wing, Lomax was intelligently used as an aerial threat off box kicks and showed he could break the defensive line when chiming in during first-phase attack.

Zac Lomax (centre) had his second start for the Force against the Waratahs. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Two starts for the Force should not guarantee Wallabies selection, however, Lomax is making progress only two months after switching from league.

The Force's win keeps it in the hunt for a finals berth, despite occupying 10th spot on the standings with 18 points and a 4-6 (win-loss) record.

The team are seven points outside the top six, ahead of three matches at home during the final four rounds of the regular season.

The Waratahs are also in finals contention, as they are in eighth place on the standings with 20 points.

Pietsch perfect for Force

As Lomax's code switch continues to attract attention, one of his Force teammates has quietly gone about his business.

Dylan Piestch was superb for the Force against the Waratahs, scoring two tries and getting through a mountain of work on the opposite wing to Lomax.

Dylan Pietsch played a starring role for the Force in its win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Pietsch's game has reached new heights at the Force since he moved west from the Waratahs after the 2024 Super Rugby Pacific season.

He has become a world-class winger, highlighted by solid performances for the Wallabies last year.

The talk about who will be the Wallabies' first-choice wing pairing at the 2027 Rugby World Cup makes for an interesting debate, with Lomax and Mark Nawaqanitawase expected to be in the mix, alongside Max Jorgensen.

But Pietsch deserves to be in the conversation if he can carry his current form into next season.

Brumbies fall again

ACT Brumbies coach Stephen Larkham was reluctant to offer excuses about his side's form slump following Saturday night's 31-20 loss to the Queensland Reds in Brisbane.

It was the Brumbies' third straight defeat, and they dropped from fifth to sixth position on the standings with a 5-6 return from their 11 matches.

The result also meant the Brumbies were bumped off as Australia's top-ranked side in the competition, with the Reds (6-4) climbing to fourth.

Larkham faced an uphill battle before the season started, knowing he would be without Wallabies Noah Lolesio, Len Ikitau and Tom Hooper following their overseas moves.

No team in Super Rugby Pacific can lose talent and experience of that ilk and not feel the impact.

Tom Hooper left the Brumbies to join Exeter last year. (Getty Images/CameraSport: Bob Bradford)

The Brumbies seemed to be coping with the trio's absence when they were 5-3, but Larkham noted the fatigue of the season has taken its toll on the younger players, who have stepped into the breach.

Injuries have not helped either, with back-rower Charlie Cale (shoulder) ruled out for a lengthy period following the Brumbies' most recent win in round nine against the Highlanders.

Until his injury, Cale had been in career-best form.

The Brumbies went down 31-20 to the Reds in Brisbane. (AAP: Darren England)

The Brumbies had their chances against the Reds, having fought back on the scoreboard to seize a 21-20 lead with 25 minutes left in the match.

But the Reds finished over the top of their opponents, scoring a converted try and penalty goal to clinch victory.

It was an improved performance from the Brumbies, who were outclassed 45-12 by the Hurricanes in their previous start during Super Round.

A buoyant Force squad awaits Larkham and his troops, who will need to arrest a poor home record when the two teams meet at Canberra Stadium on Saturday night.

World.title: Accused underworld shooters far from trained assassins, defence argues
World.content:
Whoever shot Gavin "Capable" Preston dead in a hail of bullets was quick, clinical and ruthless.

The question facing a Victorian Supreme Court jury is whether those killers were Jaeden Tito and Rabii Zahabe.

Footage played to the court showed an assassination plot carried out to devastating effect on September 9, 2023.

In the space of about 10 seconds, two masked gunmen pulled up outside the Sweet Lulu's cafe, shot Preston seven times, and drove off.

Prosecutors allege Mr Tito and Mr Zahabe, both from NSW, were contract killers hired to take Preston out.

Loading...

But lawyers for the men, who have pleaded not guilty, say their clients could not have pulled off such a sophisticated hit.

As the court heard, Preston was a man with many enemies in the underworld, potentially including bikies, crime bosses and illegal tobacco kingpins.

He was a hardened criminal who had previously shot people and served jail time for killing a man.

'Completely implausible' men were shooters, lawyers argue

Anyone who wanted Preston dead would not have sent an amateur to do the job, defence barrister Daniel Sala told the jury.

"You're sending someone who knows what they're doing … you're sending someone, in my argument to you, who has experience. Who can handle the kick, who can handle these weapons," Mr Sala said.

" This is not a fun time in Vietnam or hanging out in Texas. "

Before their arrests for murder, Mr Tito and Mr Zahabe had no prior convictions for violence, the court heard.

A court sketch of Jaeden Tito and Rabii Zahabe. (Artist: Anita Lester)

Prosecutors allege the pair killed Preston and used several getaway cars afterwards, before being driven to NSW by a chauffeur.

But Paul Smallwood, Mr Zahabe's barrister, said it was "completely implausible" the men on trial could have been the shooters.

Mr Smallwood told the jury of an alternative theory — one which involved other, unknown people pulling the trigger and splitting up.

He said the jury might conclude Mr Zahabe was one of the people who travelled to NSW in the chauffeur-driven SUV after Preston's death. However, he argued, that did not mean he was one of the shooters.

CCTV footage of Gavin Preston before the shooting. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Victoria)

DNA found in getaway cars, balaclavas

A key plank of the prosecution case is DNA evidence tying Mr Zahabe and Mr Tito to several getaway vehicles and items found inside, including two balaclavas and a black glove.

The defence argued that did not prove the men were wearing the items as part of the shooting.

They also seized upon police testing of bullets at the crime scene, which had no detectable traces of Mr Tito or Mr Zahabe's DNA.

At best, the defence lawyers argued, the pair might have been involved in moving getaway cars into place before Preston's death.

"That's not the guy you give a gun to for a public execution," Mr Sala said of his client, Mr Tito.

Jaeden Tito is one of the men accused of killing underworld figure Gavin Preston. (Supplied)

Prosecutors concede they do not know who allegedly ordered the hit on Preston, nor identified others who assisted the shooters before and after the execution.

Preston's friend, AJ Maghnie, was seated next to him at the cafe and suffered a gunshot wound to the abdomen during the ambush.

'Murder on their minds and guns in their hands'

Crown prosecutor Kristie Churchill SC said it was true Preston had many underworld enemies, but the evidence showed Mr Tito and Mr Zahabe "pulled the trigger".

"They both had murder on their minds and guns in their hands when they killed Gavin Preston and attempted to kill Mr Maghnie," she said.

One of the shooters, face obscured, was captured on security footage setting a getaway car on fire, with flames from the explosion catching them on the arm as they fled.

In the days after Preston's death, prosecutors said numerous pictures of Mr Tito were taken by his girlfriend, which showed one of his arms bandaged.

Mr Sala said the injury was not a burn from an explosion, but a friction burn from an old bike accident.

The Crown alleged Mr Zahabe used his phone to search "no extradition countries", looked up Islamic religious passages about seeking forgiveness, and had a picture of the dead man and his fiancee.

But his lawyer said those actions were "consistent with a sense of dread" from fearing he would be accused of a crime he did not commit.

The shooting occurred in broad daylight outside a cafe in Keilor East. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Mr Zahabe, who had the nickname Rabz, was arrested on October 10, 2023.

Hours later, Mr Tito allegedly texted an associate: "Hey brother it's j rabz coey you free tonight".

"The text sent by Mr Tito is effectively an admission that he is a co-offender," the prosecutor, Ms Churchill, said.

"There's no other reasonable way to interpret that message."

Having heard evidence over three weeks, the jury is receiving final instructions from Justice Michael O'Connell before retiring to consider verdicts in the case.

World.title: Vietnam's 135,000-seat gold stadium points to something even bigger
World.content:
It could hold 135,000 spectators and looks like a giant Vietnamese drum.

Right now, it is a 24-hour construction site, but by 2030, proponents say Hung Vuong Stadium will be one of the world's biggest arenas.

On paper, it has 3,000 more seats than the Narendra Modi Stadium in India, and will rival North Korea's Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, which is estimated to hold between 114,000 and 150,000 people.

The developer, Vingroup, has said it would have the world's biggest retractable roof and was planned as part of a 925 trillion dong ($53 billion) Olympic sports park in southern Hanoi.

Multiple stadiums are included in the proposed sporting precinct that will be the centrepiece of a larger development housing up to 1.2 million people.

Vingroup says the stadium will be the biggest FIFA-approved soccer facility in the world. (Supplied: Vingroup)

The stadium was first called Lac Viet, in honour of the ancient indigenous people of Vietnam's north, before being changed to Trong Dong, in honour of its design that references Dong Son drums.

In late April, Vingroup announced it would be called Hung Vuong Stadium, in honour of the ancient founders and rulers of the first Vietnamese state.

It is part of Vietnam's push to reshape its future through what one expert describes as an era of infrastructure "fever".

Vietnam's construction boom

At a cost of more than 5 quadrillion dong, or about $280 billion, Vietnam announced or broke ground on some 550 infrastructure projects in 2025 alone, including 234 on a single day in December.

Construction began on the country's first bullet train line in April, a 120-kilometre track between Hanoi and Ha Long, which will allow trains to travel up to 350 kilometres per hour.

An artist's impression of a proposed high-speed rail train station at Ha Long Bay in Vietnam. (Supplied: Vingroup)

Proponents say it will cut travel time from more than two hours to under 30 minutes and cost 157 trillion dong ($8.2 billion), excluding land acquisition costs.

The government also wants to start work this year on a second high-speed rail line that would cover 1,541km from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City, despite no feasibility study.

The project would cut the journey from 30 hours to under six, while also transporting goods and serving defence purposes, according to state media reports.

Vingroup pulled its bid to build the 1.7 quadrillion dong ($94 billion) project in December.

Around-the-clock work is ongoing to try to meet the construction deadline of 2030. (Supplied: VTC News)

Hundreds more projects are planned, including the country's first nuclear power plants, highway expansions, airports and rail projects.

The government has borrowed heavily to bring the plans to life, including from private investors and from the mega-conglomerate, Vingroup.

Nguyen Khac Giang, visiting fellow in the Vietnam studies program at Singapore's Yusof Ishak Institute, said Communist Party General Secretary and recently elected president To Lam was leading the infrastructure boom.

"Lam really wants to put his signature on building something big, something grandiose, to mark what he calls a new era of 'national rise' in Vietnam," Dr Nguyen said.

"The population is growing, and the demand is growing. So, I don't think Vietnam can afford having less infrastructure. The thing is that you have to prioritise.

"Maybe now you don't need a lot of stadiums."

Some locals who were paid to make the Olympic park a reality agree.

Many farmers were paid for their land to allow the development to happen. (AFP: Nhac Nguyen)

Chung was paid nearly 2 billion dong ($105,700) for his farmland by stadium developer Vingroup to allow the development to go ahead.

"I don't think Vietnam can host a [soccer] World Cup, so what's the use of the world's largest stadium here?" he told AFP.

"We can never benefit from that huge stadium. There will be no jobs there for us."

But economic growth is exactly what Mr Lam wants.

China funding infrastructure plans

Many of the projects being pushed forward had stalled before Mr Lam took office.

He told senior Communist Party members this year that the country "cannot accept low economic growth", as he aims to turn Vietnam into an upper-middle-class economy by 2030.

To achieve that, Vietnam will need to raise its GPD per capita by 70 per cent from the current figure of 135 million dong ($6,900).

The long-term goal agreed to by the ruling Communist Party is to turn the country into a high-income economy by 2045.

Vietnam has turned to other countries, including the US and China, for funding.

Hanoi is planning to build two rail lines to China as part of the Two Corridors, One Belt initiative, which connects to China's global Belt and Road infrastructure program.

To Lam visited Xi Jinping in Beijing last month before the funding announcement was made. (Shen Hong/Xinhua via AP)

Dr Nguyen said people in Vietnam were wary of China's influence, with the finance deal a potential sovereignty risk and debt trap.

He said the infrastructure projects should be managed "with more caution than speed" to ensure Vietnam could handle the project costs now and the inevitable repayment.

Vingroup is set to develop the Olympic park with multiple stadiums, golf courses and residential areas. (Supplied: Vingroup)

Thang Nam Do, deputy director of the Vietnam Policy Studies Hub at Australian National University, said the country made sweeping changes to 86 laws last year, from foreign investment to project approval, to help attract foreign investment.

Relying too heavily on external funding sources came with risks, he said, but added that it appeared they had been effectively mitigated.

"They are reforming the regulations to provide an environment for projects to proceed more smoothly," Dr Do told the ABC.

"The investors will see it as an enabling investment environment more than the risky one, and hence, it's likely that the foreign investor will flow in."

Can Vietnam meet its targets?

Only time will tell whether Vietnam can pull off its huge program of major infrastructure works on schedule and on budget.

Vietnam has a history of major infrastructure projects running significantly behind schedule.

Local media reported last month that labour shortages were making it hard to complete work at sites needed for next year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

To Lam wins second term to rule Vietnam through 2030 Vietnam's leader To Lam has been re-appointed as head of the ruling Communist Party for the next five years.

Ho Chi Min City's second metro line broke ground in January this year, 16 years after it was first approved.

It also withdrew from hosting the Asian Games in 2019, citing budget restraints after winning the bid to host the event in Hanoi.

Dr Do said the country had set a goal of 10 per cent GDP growth year on year, which would surpass the World Bank's projection that a 7-8 per cent annual rise would help it meet its 2045 high-income economy target.

Plans to modernise the economy and export markets would help, alongside the focus on infrastructure, he added.

"What we observe is a strong ambition, a clear implementation road map, and concrete measures to work toward it," he said.

ABC/AFP

World.title: Australian government sued over treatment of teen with disability
World.content:
A teenager with multiple disabilities stranded for days in Vanuatu's capital city after a deadly 2024 earthquake is taking the Australian government to the federal court for disability discrimination.

Sean Senbel-Lynch — who lives with cerebral palsy, a visual impairment and epilepsy — and his family allege he was refused access to the Australian Defence Force (ADF) flights used to evacuate hundreds of other Australians following the magnitude-7.3 quake.

With the Port Vila airport closed to commercial flights in the immediate aftermath, Sean's father Liam Lynch said he repeatedly appealed to Australian authorities for help to evacuate his son.

Mr Lynch, who was in Australia at the time, said he was told by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) it had been informed by the ADF that evacuation flights were not suitable for wheelchair users.

Sean uses a manual wheelchair to help with mobility but can walk with assistance, and when he boards flights, he walks onto the plane himself and travels in a standard seat.

Sean, now aged 15, said nobody at any point asked him or his family about his disabilities.

"[There] should have been an in-person assessment of what I could do, rather than them making assumptions of what I could do," Sean said.

"All disabilities are different. Even though I might have a milder cerebral palsy, I might be able to do certain things that other people with disabilities mightn't be able to do."

Sean's father Liam Lynch tried to orchestrate his family's return to Australia from Brisbane. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Sean returned home to Brisbane on a commercial flight when the Port Vila airport reopened, five days after the earthquake struck.

He said if he was not allowed on an evacuation flight, the government should have sought the use of an air ambulance or found another way to transport him out of the danger zone.

"That's their job," Sean said.

Legal documents were filed by Sean's legal team from the Justice and Equity Centre (JEC) in the federal court last week, alleging disability discrimination occurred.

"The reason why I am going to court is because … I believe there has to be major reforms," Sean said.

JEC senior solicitor Nicola Colagiuri said Sean was unlawfully discriminated against on the basis of his disability.

"Sean was treated less favourably than people without disability when he was trying to access evacuation flights … he was left in Vanuatu for four days when almost 700 other Australians and residents were brought back home," she said.

"In our view, the Commonwealth government did not properly assess whether adjustments could have been made in Sean's case to allow him access to and travel on the defence evacuation flights."

Nicola Colagiuri says Sean was discriminated against. (ABC News: Adam Wyatt)

'I felt guilt'

Power outages immediately following the earthquake meant the daily hormone medication Sean takes to manage his growth was destroyed.

His vision impairment made it difficult to understand what was happening, while the reflexes associated with his cerebral palsy meant the aftershocks left him in a heightened state of distress.

Sean was in Vanuatu with his mother and sister, visiting his grandmother, whose home was significantly damaged in the disaster.

The earthquake caused structural damage to his grandmother's home, including a partial ceiling collapse, cracked walls and buckled floors.

The magnitude-7.3 earthquake caused serious damage to Sean's grandmother's home. (Supplied: Lynch family)

"I [felt] frustration and anger, but also guilt that had I not been in Vanuatu, my sister, my mum and my grandma would have been able to evacuate without having those burdens of and hurdles of me being there," Sean said.

Mr Lynch said he repeatedly sought clarification about who could travel on evacuation flights and why, but did not receive a clear response.

"I got a sense there was a bit of finger-pointing on DFAT's part, trying to imply that it was out of their control, that decisions were being made by the ADF as to who could or couldn't go on evacuation flights.

"I had no access to the ADF. All of my points of contact were with DFAT."

Mr Lynch said it was "absolutely apparent" to him that "they had no idea what to do with somebody in a wheelchair".

Liam Lynch feels as if nobody wanted to take responsibility for getting Sean home. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The family's plight made headlines at the time, when DFAT said it was assisting Australians stranded in Vanuatu.

That angered Mr Lynch, knowing his son was barred from the evacuation flights.

"One of the most vulnerable [people], a child with a disability, was left behind. It was my child, so I did everything humanly possible to try and get him home."

Mr Lynch said his son was a determined and resilient boy who had represented Australia internationally in para-athletics and overcome a lot in his life.

Documents alleging Sean was discriminated against due to his disability have been filed in the federal court. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Ms Colagiuri said it was incumbent on the Commonwealth to ensure that what happened to Sean did not happen to anyone else.

"Australia has experienced an unprecedented number of natural disasters domestically over the last few years. That's only going to increase here and overseas as the climate crisis worsens and geopolitical tensions rise," she said.

"What's important here is that the Commonwealth government seriously reviews its policies … to ensure that people with disability are included and properly accounted for before, during, and after emergencies."

ABC News contacted DFAT and the ADF for comment, but the government said it could not comment on a matter before the courts.

World.title: Church ordains man facing rape charge interstate as a deacon
World.content:
A man with criminal convictions for family violence who is also facing a rape charge has recently been ordained as a deacon at a northern Tasmanian church.

Mathew Murray Harrison, 41, was convicted in the Launceston Magistrates Court in October 2024 of three family violence charges, and was sentenced to four months' jail, wholly suspended for two years.

Magistrate Evan Hughes found the three counts of common assault proven.

According to the charge sheet from police, Mr Harrison attempted to headbutt the victim twice, punched her in the face, choked her and threw her.

Separately, he has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape. That case remains before the District Court in Queensland.

Mr Harrison was ordained as a deacon at the Seventh-day Adventist church in Deloraine during the service on March 28.

The roles of a deacon in the Seventh-day Adventist Church include visiting church members. (ABC News: Greg Szabo)

Deacon to lead in 'very special way'

At the service, Pastor Darryl Groves said it would be Mr Harrison's role to "come alongside of our church members and to help them to grow in their spiritual journey".

"Lord, we just want to thank you and praise you for bringing Mathew to our congregation to lead in this very special way," he said.

"So, Lord, we dedicate his life to service."

Pastor Darryl Groves (right) led a prayer during Mathew Harrison's ordination as a deacon. (YouTube: Deloraine Seventh Day Adventist Church)

According to the position description, the role of deacon within the Seventh-day Adventist Church includes the following responsibilities:

Helping with services, baptisms and meetings

Visiting church members

Helping older members of the congregation and those with disability with their mobility needs

Helping with church property care and maintenance and emergency management.

The position description also notes that it is a requirement that all deacons working in a "child-related role" have cleared a working with children check or equivalent.

In Tasmania, that means a working with vulnerable people check.

As part of this, a background check and risk assessment are done, which include a national criminal history check that looks at convictions from criminal offences, all spent convictions, any pending charges that have not yet been decided by a court, and any charges that have been finalised but that did not result in a conviction.

It is not clear whether Mr Harrison's role is considered "child-related" by the church.

Seventh-day Adventist Church policy stipulates that deacons in a "child-related" role must have a working with children check. (ABC News: Greg Szabo)

'Immoral and unacceptable'

Child safety reformist Hetty Johnston said the national principles for child safe organisations published by the federal government's National Office for Child Safety clearly set out what organisations should be doing when appointing people to any role.

"Part of that is that people need to have a criminal history check. They need to have a working with children check," Ms Johnston said.

"The best interests of vulnerable people are the priority when you're recruiting, particularly to roles where those roles either involve direct contact with vulnerable people and children, or whether it is a position of power, authority, or where that person could use that position to … gain access to vulnerable people, to gain trust," she said.

Ms Johnston said organisations had a "legally binding duty of care to the vulnerable people" with whom they work.

"There are serious consequences for getting this wrong," she said.

Hetty Johnston says there are clear rules for organisations when it comes to appointing people to any role. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

She said religious organisations, like the Seventh-day Adventist Church, were highlighted by the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, which handed down its final report in 2017.

"So there's no excuse for Seventh-day Adventists to not be aware of what their responsibilities are … For any organisation, including them, to ignore it, not only is it illegal, but it's immoral and it's unacceptable in any man's language," she said.

Religious organisations were highlighted by the child sexual abuse royal commission. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Church says safety 'of the utmost importance'

The ABC asked the Seventh-day Adventist Church whether the role of deacon requires a working with vulnerable people registration — or its equivalent in other states — and whether it was aware of Mr Harrison's convictions.

The church did not respond to these questions.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church communications officer provided this response:

"Local church appointments are made at a congregational level, based on an individual's current commitment to faith, service and community life," they said.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church did not respond to specific questions about Mr Harrison's appointment. (ABC News: Greg Szabo)

"Any opportunity to serve is dependent on clear accountability, appropriate processes, and evidence that an individual's conduct is consistent with the standards expected of those in positions of trust.

"The Seventh-day Adventist Church condemns all forms of violence.

"Such behaviour is completely inconsistent with the teachings of Jesus Christ and the values of our church.

"The safety, dignity and wellbeing of all individuals is of the utmost importance, and we do not tolerate abuse in any form.

"Out of respect for privacy, we do not comment on personal matters beyond this."

World.title: ‘The most powerful presence is absence’: Dorothy Porter reimagined
World.content:
CultureMusicArts ‘The most powerful presence is absence’: Dorothy Porter reimagined Will Cox May 5, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sophia Brous and Andrea Goldsmith are talking about muses. “Oh my God,” says Goldsmith. “It’s a shocking term. But did I inspire her best work? Of course!” She laughs. Goldsmith’s partner was Dorothy Porter, the revered Australian poet who passed away in 2008. Porter’s final published work, The Bee Hut (2009), is the basis for Life Lines, a new song cycle by Brous, performed with Paul Grabowsky, to premiere at the Melbourne Writers Festival. Sophia Brous (left) and Andrea Goldsmith. Ruby Alexander Nearly two decades after her death, Porter is very much the centre of the conversation. As she writes in “Egypt”, the opening poem of The Bee Hut, “The most powerful presence is absence.” Life Lines is part of Brous’ Set Pieces series of song cycles inspired by poets. The libretto is written in advance from existing works, but the music emerges through improvisation.



Past performances have been built from the words of Argentinian Russian-Jewish poet Alejandra Pizarnik and Polish poet Debora Vogel. It was Veronica Sullivan, director of the Melbourne Writers Festival, who suggested she turn her eye to Dorothy Porter. Notes and deliberations about the show, inspired by the work of the late Dorothy Porter, one of Australia’s most revered poets. Ruby Alexander “She’s such a revered figure in the psyche of the country, and in my own psyche,” says Brous. “I said, ‘Sure, but ... am I allowed? Is that OK?’” It was. She met with Goldsmith, guardian of Porter’s work, who gave her approval to the piece, and lent the title, Life Lines. After Brous and Goldsmith met and settled on the poems that would form the piece, Brous recalls getting an email from Goldsmith. “It said, ‘You should, you do with this work what you wish,’” which is incredible,” says Brous.



“Which Dot would have said too,” says Goldsmith. “She was always a very generous collaborator. She loved what another artist could bring to her words.” One of Australia’s most influential poets, Porter is best known for her 1994 verse novel, The Monkey’s Mask, which has been adapted for stage, radio and film. Music was always an influence on her work, and vice versa. This latest project, Goldsmith says, is exactly the sort of thing Porter would have loved. Related Article Literature How Shaun Tan’s book with no storyline inspired so many tattoos “From the very beginning, composers have recognised how musical Dot’s poetry is,” says Goldsmith. “There’s something about her words, and as you read them you can actually feel the musicality.” Porter collaborated with Grabowsky for the 2005 album Before Time Could Change Us, with vocals by Katie Noonan. Since Porter’s death, Goldsmith has overseen several musical collaborations based on the poet’s work. A collaboration with Tim Finn which Porter began in the 1990s finally premiered in 2016 as The Fiery Maze. Further musical adaptations of her work have been performed by Jonathan Mills and Brett Dean.



Brous has known Grabowsky for years, and sought him out to collaborate on this project even before she had settled on Porter as the piece’s inspiration. That he’d worked with Porter came as a surprise. “I believe in creative, in the serendipity of things,” says Brous. Porter often wrote to music, too. Goldsmith shows us a playlist that Porter made for her of the songs she had in mind while writing The Bee Hut. It’s the first time Brous has seen it. It’s an eclectic list, full of big feelings, from AC/DC to Antony and the Johnsons. “I would ask Dot about the music that she used, because I could so rarely see a connection with the writing,” says Goldsmith. “It operated at a very visceral level for her. It took her out of herself.” Brous is a musician who lives between Melbourne and New York, where she is part of the improvisational band Exo-Tech, formed with Kiwi musician Kimbra.



“This project, for me, is a way of playfully subverting audience’s expectations,” says Brous. “I’d be very happy if no one in the audience knows that the piece is being created in the moment. It doesn’t matter.” Poet Dorothy Porter. Cathryn Tremain The collection that Brous was most drawn to, The Bee Hut, is an intimate book which grapples with mortality and loss. “But it has a certain giddy romance throughout as well,” says Brous. No two performances of Life Lines will be alike, but Brous is uneasy about the word “improv”, which carries jazz connotations, or “jam”, which sounds too loose. “We’re letting the words be the scenery, the environments around the text,” says Brous. The term “emergent composition” sits well, as does Brous’ comparison to American artist Alexander Calder’s hanging mobiles. It implies balance, movement. “It’s a dance,” says Brous. “We’re in a dialogue that is emergent, and that takes a great deal of trust and relinquishing of control as well.”



Goldsmith is excited about the possibilities. “What is actually going to happen on the night is going to be a real surprise to me,” she says. “I mean, of course I know Paul’s music, and now I know Sophia’s, but it’s emerging in the moment. It’s quite extraordinary.” She once saw Grabowsky perform an improvisation based on the Goldberg Variations. “He started in a known place, and he ended in a known place, and he took on a journey that Bach would have been proud of,” she says. “It was unbelievable.” Goldsmith believes in seeing Porter’s work take on new forms. She once wrote that Porter wanted to see poetry “displayed in neon”. “She was a typical poet, in that she saw poetry as the pinnacle of writing,” says Goldsmith. “Her aim was to bring poetry from the back of the shop, where it was mouldering with the craft books, up to the window.” “In this series so far, I’ve worked with writing that I had no personal connection to, but this has been a much more personal process,” Brous says. “And to have Dot’s partner – in life and in creativity - able to talk me through every single poem … I’ve never experienced this kind of intimacy as a background.” Life Lines is at the State Library of Victoria on Friday, as part of Melbourne Writers Festival.

World.title: ASX set to fall, oil jumps on war uncertainty; RBA decision ahead; GameStop makes $78b bid for eBay
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall, oil jumps on war uncertainty; RBA decision ahead; GameStop makes $78b bid for eBay Stan Choe May 5, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is falling from its record heights while oil prices jump following escalations in the Middle East that may be undermining the ceasefire in the war with Iran. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent, coming off its latest all-time high. The Dow Jones was down 528 points, or 1.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.2 per cent lower. Wall Street has fallen to start the week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 4.53am AEST pointing to a fall of 75 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Monday. The Reserve Bank announces its interest rates decision on Tuesday afternoon, with higher inflation expected to force the central bank to inflict a third consecutive hike. Financial markets put the chance of a rate rise at 75 per cent with at least one more increase expected by October. The overnight action was strong in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude leaped 5.6 per cent to $US114.21. It jolted higher after the United Arab Emirates said it came under attack by Iran for the first time since the fragile ceasefire took hold in early April. The attacks appeared to be in response to US President Donald Trump’s latest efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.



Iran’s closure of the strait has kept oil tankers pent up in the Persian Gulf and away from customers worldwide. That in turn has sent the price of Brent soaring from roughly $US70 per barrel before the war. Trump said Sunday that the United States would guide ships through the strait, which could get oil flowing again and bring down its price. But prices instead climbed after Iranian news agencies claimed Monday that Iran had struck a US Navy vessel southeast of the Strait of Hormuz, accusing it of “violating maritime security and navigation norms.” The US military rejected the claim and then said that two American-flagged merchant ships had successfully transited through the Strait of Hormuz. Even with all the uncertainty about how long the war with Iran will last, the US stock market has managed to power to record after record. Hope is still high on Wall Street that the global economy can avoid a worst-case scenario because of the war. And in the meantime, companies continue to deliver big growth in profits. That’s key because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. The strength so far this reporting season has been broad-based and not confined to just the Big Tech superstars that dominate the market. The median stock in the S&P 500 is tracking for the best growth since 2021, according to Savita Subramanian, a strategist at Bank of America.



Tyson Foods joined the list Monday of those topping analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue during the latest quarter. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America The cracks are widening in Trump’s America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist It sold less beef than it did a year ago, but it did so at prices that were 11.5 per cent higher, so its total beef revenue edged up. It also sold more chicken and pork than a year earlier, at slightly higher prices. Its stock rose 3.9 per cent. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings likewise delivered a better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. But it’s feeling the effects of the war, which has not only raised pressure on fuel prices but also pushed some customers to think twice about travel plans, particularly to Europe. The cruise operator said some “execution missteps” also have bookings below where it would like, and its stock fell 9.2 per cent.



GameStop slumped after it said it wants to buy eBay for about $US56 billion ($78 billion) in cash and stock, an offer that . Coming into the day, eBay had a total market value that was nearly quadruple GameStop’s. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing Seven’s Game of Thrones claims another victim Colin Kruger Senior business reporter GameStop said it has already built a 5 per cent stake in eBay and sees opportunities to cut $US2 billion in annual costs quickly. GameStop, whose stock briefly soared to market-shaking heights during the meme stock craze of 2021, fell 7.8 per cent, while eBay rose 5.7 per cent. Several Big Tech stocks were strong, continuing a big run for companies involved in artificial-intelligence technology. Micron Technology gained 5.8 per cent for one of the biggest gains in the S&P 500. Oracle rallied 5.7 per cent, and Sandisk climbed 4.4 per cent. In stock markets abroad, gains for tech stocks helped indexes jump 5.1 per cent in South Korea and 1.2 per cent in Hong Kong, while markets were closed in mainland China and Japan for holidays.



European indexes fared worse, and France’s CAC 40 fell 1.7 per cent. In the bond market, Treasury yield jumped up as oil prices climbed. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.45 per cent from 4.39 per cent late on Friday. It was at just 3.97 per cent before the war began, and the rise has made mortgages and other kinds of loans for US households and businesses more expensive. World.title: ‘Inexplicable’: Why Casey-style council corruption could happen again
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In Wollongong, it was council planners trading developer approvals for cash, sex and luxury handbags. Closer to home in Melbourne’s sprawling City of Casey, there were allegations of cash drops in brown paper bags in suburban Subway outlets and political schmoozing at soirees in Chinatown’s Flower Drum restaurant. In both instances, authorities allege money was spent to buy outcomes. In NSW, following the sensational Operation Atlas corruption probe which saw the entire Wollongong council sacked, the state banned donations by property developers to politicians and local councillors in 2009 – within a year of the allegations being aired. Former Casey mayor Sam Aziz (left) and developer John Woodman in a Subway outlet in 2018. But in Victoria, eight years after the anti-corruption watchdog launched an inquiry into Casey council and almost three years after its damning Operation Sandon report on the scandal, there has been no wholesale crackdown on developer donations in local government. In December, the Allan government had a clear chance to end the integrity headaches plaguing Victorian councils through its new planning bill, where it had the opportunity to cap or ban donations from developers to councillors. Instead, the government ignored two formal levels of expert advice and explicitly refused to stem the flow of developer money. There are still those pushing for change. The state’s anti-corruption watchdog, IBAC, says there is more work to do and its former commissioner, Robert Redlich, KC, says the state has not done enough to prevent the next corruption scandal.



Councillors who operate within the rules are saddled with so many potential conflicts of interest they are repeatedly required to recuse themselves from important votes. And it seems everyone – including some incumbent City of Melbourne councillors – agrees the current settings are far from best-practice governance. Lord Mayor Nick Reece moved a motion last year to call on the state government to consider reforms, which was supported by the council. “I am on the record multiple times advocating for donation reform in local government and improvements to the City of Melbourne Act,” he said. “I am hopeful we will see new rules in place for the next local government elections.” But as it stands, when it comes to big-developer money in local councils – it’s business as usual. A squibbed opportunity for reform Reece and his “Team Nick” group of councillors raised $950,484 for the 2024 City of Melbourne election campaign. This was three times the amount his predecessor Sally Capp raised for her final campaign. Team Reece donations were forthcoming from a who’s who of Melbourne, including wealthy business people, trade unions and people who own large amounts of property in the City of Melbourne.



Reece and his team were able to do this entirely within the existing rules, and there is no suggestion of impropriety on the part of the candidates or donors. Indeed, Reece went further than the law required him to by seeking to limit donations from property developers, which in some other states would be disallowed entirely. Many other candidates made no such attempts. “Team Kouta”, fronted by former AFL star Anthony Koutoufides, received $325,280 from property developer Intaj Khan, who was running alongside the footballer for the position of deputy mayor. That accounted for almost 70 per cent of donations to Koutoufides’ failed mayoral tilt. Khan’s contribution would be impossible in South Australia, NSW and, until recently, Queensland, but was entirely legal under Victorian law. The state is now a stark outlier in Australian integrity standards. In NSW and Queensland, individual donations are capped at $3900 and $7200 respectively. In NSW and the ACT, developer donations are entirely banned. Queensland had also outlawed developer donations, but the Crisafulli LNP government recently overturned the ban. In these jurisdictions, a property developer is broadly defined as an individual or corporation engaged in a business that regularly makes “relevant planning applications” for residential or commercial development with the ultimate goal of profit.



To prevent developers from using family members or satellite companies to funnel money, these jurisdictions use a “close associate” rule. This effectively broadens the ban to include the developer’s directors, officers, and their spouses. South Australia has moved even further at a state level, implementing a world-first blanket ban on almost all political donations to candidates, parties and sitting MPs, although that prohibition does not yet extend to local councils. Still, for local elections in SA, individual donations to local candidates are capped at $5000 per year, with any gift over $2500 requiring real-time public disclosure within five days. This is far from the case in Victoria. Here, while a $4970 limit has existed for state government elections (at least until the High Court recently upended the state’s electoral funding laws), council-level donations – where the vast majority of planning decisions are made – remain entirely unlimited. Former IBAC commissioner Robert Redlich, KC, says the state has not done enough to prevent the next corruption scandal. AAP Redlich, the former IBAC commissioner who led the Operation Sandon investigation, told The Age the government’s refusal to match state-level caps at the local level was inexplicable. “There really hasn’t been a satisfactory explanation by government for why, in the case of councils, caps are not necessary,” said Redlich, who now sits on the board of non-partisan integrity advocacy group the Accountability Round Table.



Related Article Exclusive

IBAC Labor, Nationals argue against developer donation ban “There are even more compelling reasons why caps should exist at local government level as unlike MPs at state level, councillors are not only influencers, they are the decision-makers to whom the donor has direct access.” Operation Sandon, the longest-running corruption probe in the state’s history into the Casey scandal, was supposed to be the catalyst for change. In 2022, the corruption watchdog recommended local government donations be capped and to match the state level limits. A year later, its Operation Sandon report went further, calling for serious consideration of a total ban on donations from “high-risk groups” including property developers – repeating a call from former Victorian Ombudsman Deborah Glass in 2015. The then-Daniel Andrews led government referred IBAC’s 2022 recommendations to an expert panel. That panel suggested a ban might be unnecessary – provided political finance laws were “sufficiently robust” and included a cap. In October, the Allan government promised its new planning bill would finally address the recommendations from the Sandon report. However, the bill that passed in December includes neither a ban nor a cap. It merely includes a new disclosure requirement– which critics say was rushed, clunky and fails to seriously mitigate the risk of corruption.

World.title: From 119 students to 1445 in five years: The Sydney suburb that exploded before schools arrived
World.content:
Raj and Aman Mangat with their youngest daughter Iskara (and dog, Simba) outside their home in Box Hill in Sydney’s northwestern suburbs.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney’s infrastructure has long failed to keep up with its growth. We examine where the biggest deficits are now. See all stories .

Like most families who move to Box Hill in north-western Sydney, Aman Mangat, her husband Raj and their two daughters were attracted to the suburb’s large homes and community feel. But there was just one thing missing: schools. With no public high school in Box Hill that teaches past year seven, Aman’s eldest daughter Amlina, who is in year 12, commutes to a private school in Parramatta. And while the youngest daughter Iskara travels a shorter distance – 20 minutes by car to a school in Schofields to avoid the demountables at Box Hill primary – it means someone must be available every day to pick her up. “We can’t have that leisure of her walking home,” Aman said. “It’s eating into our time a lot.” In 2018, the former NSW Liberal government released plans for four new public schools in Box Hill, but those plans never came to fruition. The Labor government installed a temporary primary school in 2025 and a temporary high school in 2026 that caters for year seven only, with year eight to commence in 2027. Aravind Vijay stands outside the temporary public school in Box Hill. Wolter Peeters Father of two Aravind Vijay, who successfully campaigned for the suburb’s temporary primary school, was left “dumbstruck” after being told his eldest son would not be able to attend because their home sits just outside the catchment. It means the family will have to undertake a 45-minute round trip to the over-capacity Rouse Hill Public School, passing the local school that’s just 10 minutes away. The Mangats and Vijays are among tens of thousands of Australian families who have moved into Sydney’s newest suburbs in the north-west and south-west, lured by the promise of world-class schools – only to find the schools have been cancelled or delayed. As the population booms in these greenfield sites and more homes are built, residents are finding vital infrastructure remains an afterthought.



When the Herald visits on the first day of term one, the entrance to the Box Hill temporary primary school is full of nervous parents waiting to pick up their children. In front of them is a sea of grey demountables tightly packed together. There are no trees, and the rear of the school is still under construction. In 2018, the Box Hill-Nelson area had 119 total student enrolments. Five years later, that number exploded to 1445 – an increase of 1114 per cent – the NSW Enrolment Growth Audit says. The demountables at the temporary Box Hill public primary school. Wolter Peeters A permanent Box Hill primary and high school will open in 2028 at a new site in Box Hill, and the NSW Labor government has bought the land of the temporary school to turn it into a permanent one. A spokesperson for the NSW Department of Education did not say when this would happen, but said the government would “continue to monitor demographic trends and student population projections” to determine when to build a new school. When the Box Hill precinct was rezoned in 2013, it was expected to accommodate 9600 homes and 28,000 people. In the next decade, The Hills Shire Council estimates the number of residents to soar to 50,000. The council, which also covers greenfield sites such as the Gables and North Kellyville, has warned that The Hills will need 15 more new public schools to keep up with the population. It’s not just a problem in The Hills: western Sydney is expected to grow in population by 32 per cent between 2026 and 2046, compared with 13 per cent in most eastern and inner-city areas, according to the Centre for Western Sydney. With more people moving to Sydney’s west, the question remains: will there be enough schools?



‘Lessons have not been learnt’ A 2022 inquiry into the planning and delivery of school infrastructure in NSW found that poor demographic planning had resulted in schools in high-growth areas reaching and exceeding their capacity in unacceptably short time frames – particularly greenfield areas in Sydney’s south-west and north-west. It has led to many students having to undertake “longer-than-acceptable commutes” to the next nearest school, more families turning to private schools or children having to attend schools that don’t have adequate facilities to cope with the high number of enrolments. No schools better encapsulate these planning mistakes than the Ponds High School – which was reported as having more than double its enrolment cap in 2025 and is the biggest public school in the state – and the early years of Oran Park Public School in the south-west. The first primary school in the suburb, Oran Park Public School had 11 kindergarten classes when it opened in 2014. That number swelled to 21 classes just seven years later. The same school had 13 demountables in 2015, but by 2020 that number was 27. The 2022 inquiry said the former state government had tried to manage demand for Oran Park Public School – which had about 1500 students and was 40 per cent over capacity at the time – by reducing the catchment boundaries, to the extent that the school primarily drew from one street in the local area. “The local community has compared the demountables to the look of Manus Island, and it is clear that the school’s development was a demographic planning disaster,” the report said.



Oran Park had no public high school until 2020, with the Herald reporting last year that Oran Park High eclipsed 1600 students just five years after opening. Rows of demountables at NSW’s biggest public school, The Ponds High. Edwina Pickles But there have been some improvements for schools in the suburb – today, the number of students enrolled at Oran Park Public School has decreased to 1380 and there are no demountables. Related Article Stranded Sydney The Rajs bought into the Australian dream. It came with a nightmare Deputy Premier and Minister for western Sydney Prue Car said the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s recently released report into School Infrastructure NSW found staff were asked to alter population data, with the “effect of diverting funds from north-west and south-west Sydney”. Car said the Labor government is now delivering the new and upgraded schools these communities need. “We have also reformed the way school infrastructure is planned and delivered to ensure best practice and that schools are built where they are needed most,” she said.

World.title: The pro secret that gives Mamasita’s famous fish tacos their crunch
World.content:
Mamasita's fish tacos are built on made-to-order masa tortillas and finished with plenty of lime. Joe Armao

The fish taco is a Mamasita mainstay – a refined evolution of the dish that hit the menu when the Melbourne restaurant opened in February 2010. It has been a crowd favourite for more than 16 years, proving that while trends come and go, a masterfully executed taco is non-negotiable.

The secret is the crunch: firm white fish – think snapper or monkfish – is coated in a spiced, gluten-free batter. Using GF flour isn’t just for dietary needs; the starches produce a superior crispness, says executive chef Jimmy Garside.

Mamasita executive chef Jimmy Garside. Joe Armao

The dish features house-made masa tortillas, pressed to order, layered with smoky chipotle glaze, jalapeno crema, and plenty of lime for zing. To master the flow at home, prepare the glaze and masa dough a day ahead.

Just before serving, whip up the crema and garnishes. “The big thing with Mexican food is freshness,” Garside says. “Once you cut the chillies, herbs and onions, they start to lose flavour.”

The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up

For best results, source authentic Mexican oregano and Tajín, a tangy chilli-lime-salt seasoning, from specialist grocers such as Poblano Mexican in Melbourne’s Cheltenham, and Fireworks Foods in Sydney.

Whether served as an interactive family dinner or a light starter paired with a zesty cabbage salad, these tacos deliver an ideal balance of golden crunch, earthy spice and citrus-bright heat.

World.title: One of the world’s biggest cities is a surprising hiking heaven
World.content:
InspirationAdventure holidays One of the world’s biggest cities is a surprising hiking heaven Rob McFarland May 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the things I expected to find in Seoul, fabulous hiking wasn’t one of them. Which is surprising given how successful Korea has been in exporting so many aspects of its culture, from kimchi and K-pop to skin care and K-dramas. Inwangsan Mountain. Seoullo 7017, a former highway overpass. Dig beneath the city’s high-tech facade and you’ll discover a wide variety of trails, from gentle city-centre ambles to challenging mountain ascents. There are also excellent facilities, in the form of three dedicated tourist hiking centres with knowledgeable staff, changing rooms, lockers and a rental service for boots, backpacks and clothing. Start your exertions gently with a stroll along Seoullo 7017, a one-kilometre elevated walkway near Seoul Station. Opened in 2017 on a former highway overpass, this inviting urban trail is dotted with sculptures, play areas, cafes and more than 20,000 shrubs and plants. Accessible 24/7, it’s especially beguiling at night, when the illuminated thoroughfare offers sweeping views of Seoul’s glittering skyline.



Another popular urban trail is the Gyeongui Line Forest Park, which stretches for 6.3 kilometres from Yeonnam-dong to Munbae-dong. This narrow greenway follows the train tracks of the Japanese-built Gyeongui Line (so it’s mostly flat) and is lined with cafes, bars, bookshops and boutiques. The trendy section near Hongik University can get busy at weekends but continue south-east and you’ll pass through tranquil pockets of verdant loveliness enroute to the moving War Memorial of Korea. 



Now you’re well and truly warmed up, it’s time for the big one: Bukhansan Mountain. Located north of the city in Bukhansan National Park, Seoul’s highest peak can be accessed from a variety of trails that all converge at Baegunbongammun Fortress gate. From here, it’s a testing scramble up a steep granite slope to the 836-metre-high summit (there are railings to help) where your efforts are rewarded with a captivating 360-degree panorama of the city. If you’ve got time, we recommend starting at the Bukhansanseong Fortress entrance (take the subway to Gupabal Station then the 704 bus) and choosing the longer summit route via Bukhansan Shelter (amusingly signposted the “easy course”). It’s quieter and has less thigh-destroying stairs. Enjoy lunch on the rocky plateau near the summit then exit the park via the eastern entrance near Bukhansan Ui station where the descent is shorter and more scenic. The big one: Bukhansan Mountain. If you’re up for a real challenge, there’s always Seoul Trail 2.0, a 157-kilometre route that circumnavigates the city. Split into 21 themed sections, each trailhead can be reached by public transport and there’s even a Seoul Trail stamp book with 28 stamps to collect along the way. Now that’s a K-hike.
